questions.enonce_markdown:
3. (a) Differentiate between physical and chemical weathering.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Weathering** is the breakdown of rock where it lies (in place), without transport by an agent of erosion.

**Physical (mechanical) weathering** is the **breaking up of rock into smaller pieces without any change in its chemical composition** (the minerals stay the same). It is caused by temperature changes (heating by day and cooling by night makes the rock expand and contract, so it cracks and flakes: exfoliation), **freeze-thaw** (water freezes in cracks and expands), crystallisation of salts, release of pressure and the growth of roots. It is common in hot deserts and in cold mountain areas.

**Chemical weathering** is the **decay (decomposition) of rock by chemical reactions, which change its minerals** into new substances. Rain water, which contains dissolved carbon dioxide (a weak acid) and oxygen, reacts with the minerals by **solution, carbonation, hydrolysis, oxidation and hydration**. For example, limestone is dissolved by carbonation, and iron-rich rocks become rusty red by oxidation. It is most active in warm, wet regions such as the humid tropics (southern Cameroon).

| | Physical weathering | Chemical weathering |
|---|---|---|
| Process | the rock breaks into pieces | the rock rots and dissolves |
| Composition of the rock | unchanged | changed |
| Main agents | temperature change, frost, salt, roots | water, dissolved gases, acids |
| Climate where common | hot deserts, cold areas | hot, wet areas |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Study the table below that shows temperature and rainfall:

| Months | J | F | M | A | M | J | J | A | S | O | N | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature (°C) | 28 | 29 | 30 | 29 | 28 | 29 | 26 | 24 | 27 | 26 | 29 | 29 |
| Rainfall (mm) | 21 | 49 | 127 | 174 | 105 | 308 | 431 | 600 | 462 | 568 | 119 | 18 |

(i) Name the instruments used to obtain the information on the table.

(2 marks)

(ii) Using a **graph paper**, plot the temperature and rainfall graph (climograph) for the weather station.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Instruments (2 marks).**

- **Temperature:** a **thermometer** (in practice a maximum-minimum thermometer kept in a **Stevenson screen**, from which the daily mean is calculated).
- **Rainfall:** a **rain gauge**.

**(ii) The climograph (5 marks).** A climograph shows **rainfall as a bar graph** and **temperature as a line graph** on the same diagram, with the months along the bottom.

*Method:*

1. Draw a frame about 12 cm wide. Divide the horizontal axis into 12 equal parts, label them J F M A M J J A S O N D, and give the graph a title.
2. **Left axis, rainfall** (bars): scale 1 cm : 100 mm, from 0 to 700 mm (the highest value is 600 mm in August). Label it "Rainfall (mm)".
3. **Right axis, temperature** (line): scale 1 cm : 5 degrees C, from 0 to 35 degrees C (the range is 24 to 30). Label it "Temperature (°C)".
4. Draw a **bar** for each month: January 21 mm, February 49, March 127, April 174, May 105, June 308, July 431, August 600, September 462, October 568, November 119, December 18.
5. Plot a **dot** for each month's temperature (28, 29, 30, 29, 28, 29, 26, 24, 27, 26, 29, 29) and join the dots with a smooth line in a different colour.
6. Add a key (bars: rainfall; line: temperature).

![fig-1](gce-ol-geography-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

**Reading the graph (checks, calculated with Python):** the total annual rainfall is 21 + 49 + 127 + 174 + 105 + 308 + 431 + 600 + 462 + 568 + 119 + 18 = **2 982 mm**; the mean annual temperature is 334 / 12 = **27.8 °C**; the annual temperature range is 30 - 24 = **6 °C** (small). Five months (June to October) bring 2 369 mm, about 79 per cent of the year's rain; December to February are the driest months (88 mm in all). This is a **hot, very wet climate with a small temperature range and a marked dry season**, with the peak of rain in August and a second high in October.

*Marks:* title and axes (1); scales (1); bars correct (1); temperature line correct (1); neatness and key (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) "Volcanic areas have many problems yet many people are attracted to settle there." Briefly explain this situation.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The problems of volcanic areas (3 marks).**

1. **Eruptions are dangerous:** lava flows, ash falls, hot gases and flying rocks destroy houses, farms, roads and kill people and animals.
2. **Other hazards:** earthquakes before and during an eruption, **mudflows (lahars)** when rain or melting snow mixes with ash, landslides on steep slopes, and poisonous gases (sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide).
3. **Loss and displacement:** eruptions may force people to leave, and rebuilding costs a lot; the steep ground makes farming and building difficult.

**Why people still settle there (3 marks).**

1. **Fertile soils:** weathered lava and volcanic ash form very fertile soils, rich in minerals, which give high yields of crops such as coffee, bananas, tea, oil palm and vegetables (for example around Mount Cameroon and in the Western Highlands of Cameroon).
2. **Other resources and attractions:** **geothermal energy** and hot springs (Iceland, Kenya), **tourism** (the climbing of Mount Cameroon, Mount Etna), building materials (basalt, pumice) and sometimes minerals; the highlands also have cool, healthy climates and good rainfall.
3. **Risk is accepted:** eruptions are rare (the memory of the last one fades), they can be monitored and forecast better today, people have lived on the volcano for generations and may have little other good land because of population pressure.

**Conclusion:** the rich soils and other benefits are seen as worth the risk of a rare disaster.

(The Mount Cameroon volcano has erupted several times in recent decades, for example in 1999, 2000 and 2012, and farming and towns continue on its slopes.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Name **THREE** stores and **THREE** outputs in the hydrological cycle.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Three stores (any three):** the **oceans and seas**; **lakes and rivers** (surface water); **ice caps and glaciers**; **groundwater** (water in the rocks, the water table); **soil moisture**; **vegetation** (water held in plants); the **atmosphere** (water vapour and clouds).

**Three outputs (any three):** **evaporation** (from the sea, lakes, rivers and soil); **transpiration** (from plants), together called evapotranspiration; **surface run-off and river discharge** into the sea; **groundwater flow** out to the sea (and, from the atmosphere, precipitation is the main input).
